A also renames Delete to "Delete project" and lightens the red while claiming copy and palette are unchanged. B keeps the copy and colours as they were, makes no inaccurate claims, and clearly lists Escape and focus handling as not done. It falls short on item 3 but is the tidier, more accurate fix the request asked for. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers fix contrast well, use real buttons with focus rings, and tone down the animation the same way. B goes further on behavior: it adds Escape handling and Cancel autofocus. But its Escape listener is always active, even when the dialog is closed, and autofocus is unreliable on a dialog that is shown dynamically. B also changes the copy ('Delete project') and the Delete color, which goes against the 'tidied, not redesigned' request. A stays tightly in scope, is honest about the focus and Escape work it didn't do, and closes with a cleaner list, so it edges ahead.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers fix the main contrast problems, swap the spans for real buttons with focus rings, and tone down the animation with a reduced-motion fallback. pass 1 (A=without, B=with): The two answers are close: both fix contrast, switch to real buttons with a focus ring, add alertdialog semantics, and tone down the animation with a reduced-motion fallback, but neither adds Escape-to-close or focus handling. B changes the width to min(420px, 100vw - 32px), which goes against the 'same width' constraint, though B's note on where focus should go is more specific. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers make nearly the same core fixes: readable colors, real buttons with a focus ring, alertdialog semantics, a gentler animation with a reduced-motion opt-out, and a darker backdrop. Neither adds Escape-to-close or focus handling, though A explains more precisely what that should do. samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give the same core advice: no loader on the fast path, one skeleton only after a ~200 ms delay, a minimum display time, keeping previous results visible, and never stacking two loaders. B edges ahead on what matters beyond the loader: a manual-entry fallback so checkout is never blocked, specific screen-reader announcements, aria-hidden skeleton rows, debouncing and reduced motion. A is a bit tighter and easier to act on, and neither answer covers keyboard use of the list. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): The two answers are nearly equivalent: each says to show neither loader by default, delay a single skeleton until the lookup has run for a short while, set a minimum display time, keep stale results visible, and use aria-live. A wins narrowly because it covers the failure case better for checkout: on error it offers manual address entry, never blocks checkout, and respects reduced motion. B's suggestion of an inline spinner as a compromise slightly blurs its recommendation, and neither answer covers keyboard use of the list.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers recommend showing no indicator at first, keeping previous results visible, and never using both loaders, and both give similar delay and minimum-display timings. B is more decisive: it picks one indicator, the trailing spinner, and explains why a skeleton causes layout jump when the result count varies. It also covers the no-results state and reduced motion. A splits the choice by state, which is reasonable but less clear, though it does add a useful point about stale responses. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give the same core advice: don't add both loaders, hold off showing any indicator for about 250-300 ms, keep previous results visible, and keep the indicator up for a minimum time so it doesn't flicker. A commits to a single spinner, explains why a skeleton causes layout jump, and covers no-results announcements and reduced motion. B splits skeleton and spinner by state and adds handling of stale responses and throttled-network testing. Neither covers keyboard use of the list or error states, so their strengths balance out.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers advise against loading on every keystroke and against using both loaders, and both suggest a delay threshold with a minimum display time. B handles the slow case better: it keeps the previous results visible and puts a small spinner beside the list rather than replacing it, which avoids layout shift. B also covers the no-results and error states as well as screen-reader announcements. A's choice of skeleton rows sits uneasily with keeping the previous results on screen, and A leaves out the no-results state. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers make the right call: no loader on fast lookups, one delayed indicator, a minimum display time, and not adding both. A handles the slow case more consistently. It keeps the previous results visible and puts a small spinner at the edge, which avoids layout shift, and it covers both the no-results and error states. B's delayed skeleton conflicts with its own advice to keep previous results visible, and it can cause layout shift when the number of results differs. B also doesn't cover the no-results state, though it does add useful debounce advice.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers correctly blame min-width:auto on .info combined with the nowrap name, and both stop the thumbnail, badge and button from shrinking. A's single-line ellipsis works at every width. B only handles the name below 480px, so on mid-size screens the nowrap name still spills past .info and can overlap the badge. B does cover long unbroken words better with its 2-line clamp and overflow-wrap:anywhere, but neither answer keeps truncated names readable elsewhere (for example in a title attribute) or fixes the small ⋯ tap target. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both correctly trace the problem to `min-width:auto` on the flex child combined with the nowrap name, and both stop the badge, thumbnail and button from shrinking. B's ellipsis applies at every width, so it is more robust. A's base fix with no ellipsis lets long names spill visibly over the badge at widths above its 480px breakpoint, though A's two-line clamp with `overflow-wrap:anywhere` is a nice touch. Neither answer addresses the small ⋯ tap target or keeping truncated names readable, for example with a title attribute.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers find the same cause (min-width:auto on .info combined with the nowrap name) and give essentially the same fix, including flex-shrink:0 on the fixed-size items and an optional two-line clamp for phones. A goes a little further on long content: it says to keep the full name readable with a title attribute, and it warns that an ancestor may have the same min-width problem. B's rules are slightly easier to paste as whole rules, but neither answer mentions the 28px tap target on the ⋯ button. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers find the same cause (min-width:auto on the flex:1 .info combined with nowrap) and give essentially the same fix. B goes further: it suggests a title attribute so truncated names stay readable, and warns that an ancestor flex or grid item may need min-width:0 too. Neither answer mentions that the 28px ⋯ button is too small to tap comfortably on a phone.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers find the same cause and give the same core fix: min-width:0 on .info, ellipsis on .name, and keeping the badge, thumb and ⋯ button from shrinking. B is slightly better because it explains why the badge gets squished, gives a complete line-clamp snippet, and points out that truncation hides 'via Schlossbergtunnel (scenic)' and that long German compounds can't break. Neither answer mentions the 28px ⋯ button being too small to tap, or a way (such as a title attribute) to keep truncated names readable. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers correctly blame `min-width: auto` on the flex child combined with the `nowrap` name. Both give the same working fix: `min-width: 0`, an ellipsis on the name, and no shrinking for the badge, thumb and button. A gives a complete block to paste in and a concrete two-line clamp, and it points out that truncation hides part of the name. B explains each change and adds useful checks for the viewport meta tag and a parent with a fixed width. Neither mentions the ⋯ button's small tap target, and neither suggests keeping truncated names readable elsewhere, for example with a `title` attribute.
